requirements: The core contributions of KernelBench — a framework for evaluating LMs on GPU kernel generation across 250 PyTorch AI workloads, the fast_p metric, baseline evaluations, and test-time methods (repeated sampling, iterative refinement, hardware-aware prompting) — have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The evaluation environment (NVIDIA L40S GPU, Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.5.0+cu124, CUDA 12.4) and other hardware platforms used in the paper are correctly set up.
Primary evaluation hardware (NVIDIA L40S GPU with Ada Lovelace architecture) is available and correctly identified.
Code has been implemented that detects and reports the GPU device name, and verifies it corresponds to an NVIDIA L40S for the primary evaluation runs.
Code has been implemented that queries and logs the L40S GPU properties (48 GB HBM memory, 300W power) via CUDA/PyTorch device query APIs.
The evaluation runs on a bare-metal (non-virtualized) L40S GPU node with exclusive access, ensuring no concurrent CUDA processes contaminate timing measurements.
The exact software stack versions (Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.5.0+cu124, CUDA 12.4) are installed and reproducible.
A Python 3.10 environment is provided (via requirements.txt, environment.yml, Dockerfile, or equivalent) and is used to run all evaluations.
PyTorch 2.5.0 built against CUDA 12.4 (i.e., torch==2.5.0+cu124) is installed, and torch.__version__ reports this string at runtime.
CUDA Toolkit 12.4 is installed such that nvcc --version reports 12.4 and torch.version.cuda returns '12.4'.
Code has been implemented that at evaluation start-up logs Python, PyTorch, and CUDA versions, and aborts or warns if they do not match the paper's specification.
PyTorch inline CUDA extension compilation (via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline with nvcc) functions correctly in the environment.
Code has been implemented that verifies torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline can compile a trivial CUDA kernel (e.g., the elementwise_add example from the one-shot prompt) end-to-end without errors.
nvcc is reachable on PATH and can compile CUDA source files targeting the appropriate SM architecture for the L40S (compute capability sm_89).
Additional GPU platforms used for the cross-hardware generalization analysis (Section 4.4) are configured with the same software stack.
Code has been implemented that supports running the evaluation pipeline on additional GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA A10G and other GPU types referenced in Section 4.4) by parameterizing device selection.
Code has been implemented that records the GPU model (L40S, A10G, etc.) alongside each measurement so results can be attributed to the correct hardware platform.
Timing infrastructure is set up to produce stable wall-clock measurements consistent with the paper's methodology.
Code has been implemented that uses torch.cuda.Event with synchronize for wall-clock timing of nn.Module.forward, performs 3 warm-up iterations, and averages over 100 profiling trials.
The environment achieves a coefficient of variation (std/mean) of the 100 timing trials that is consistently below 3% on the L40S, matching the paper's stability claim.

The 250 KernelBench tasks partitioned into three levels (Level 1: 100 primitive operators, Level 2: 100 operator sequences, Level 3: 50 full ML architectures) are available with correct PyTorch reference implementations and input specifications.
Task file format and structure follows the KernelBench specification described in Section 3.1 and Appendix A.

Code has been implemented so that each KernelBench task is a standalone Python file containing a class named `Model` derived from `torch.nn.Module` with `__init__` and `forward` methods populated with the workload's PyTorch operations.
Code has been implemented so that each task file provides a module-level `get_inputs()` function returning the list of forward-pass input tensors of the prescribed shape and dtype for the workload.

Code has been implemented so that each task file provides a module-level `get_init_inputs()` function returning the arguments required to instantiate the `Model` class (may be an empty list when no init inputs are needed).

Task files declare tensor shapes and dtypes as module-level constants (e.g., `M`, `N`, `K`, `batch_size`) so input specifications are fixed and reproducible across runs, with only tensor values being randomized.

Executing every task's `Model` with tensors from `get_inputs()` (and initializing with `get_init_inputs()`) runs without error on the reference hardware and returns tensor outputs, verifying that all 250 reference implementations are runnable PyTorch code.
Level 1 (100 tasks) contains primitive AI operators spanning matmuls, convolutions, activations, norms, and losses.

The Level 1 directory contains exactly 100 task files, each implementing a single primitive PyTorch operation (matrix multiply, convolution, activation, normalization, loss, or similar foundational building block).
Level 1 includes matrix multiplication variants (including the K=131072 large-K matmul task shown in Appendix A) as standalone operator tasks.
Level 1 includes a group of at least 34 convolution-variant tasks (as referenced in Section 5.1.1 where DeepSeek-V3 failed on 34 conv variants).
Level 1 includes elementwise activation tasks such as GeLU (referenced in Appendix D.2 as problem 87), Softsign (problem 29), and diagonal-matmul (problem 11).
Every Level 1 task's `forward` method invokes a single primitive PyTorch operation (or its direct functional equivalent), consistent with the level's definition.
Level 2 (100 tasks) contains operator-sequence workloads combining 3-6 primitive operations that admit fusion.
The Level 2 directory contains exactly 100 task files, each implementing a sequence of multiple primitive PyTorch operations composed within a single `Model.forward()`.
Each Level 2 task combines between 3 and 6 primitive operators in its forward pass (as specified in Section 3.2).
Level 2 includes representative fusion-target sequences such as Gemm+Divide+Sum+Scaling (problem 13) and matmul-then-masked-fill-then-relu style patterns referenced in Appendix D.
Level 2 tasks include workloads combining a mainloop operator (e.g., matmul or convolution) with pointwise operators (e.g., ReLU, bias, division, scaling) as described in Section 3.2.
Level 3 (50 tasks) contains full end-to-end ML architectures sourced from popular PyTorch repositories.
The Level 3 directory contains exactly 50 task files, each implementing a full ML architecture in PyTorch.

Level 3 includes named architectures referenced in the paper such as AlexNet and MiniGPT, along with additional architectures drawn from `pytorch`, `huggingface/transformers`, and `huggingface/pytorch-image-models`.
Level 3 includes a MiniGPT-style attention block variant (problem 49 referenced in Appendix D.2) that uses a ReLU-attention pattern combining matmul, scaling, masked_fill, and ReLU.
Level 3 tasks compose multiple `nn.Module` sub-components (layers, blocks) into an end-to-end forward pass, distinguishing them from Level 2 short operator sequences.
Task counts and level partitioning match the paper exactly.
The total number of tasks across all three levels equals 250.

The three level directories are organized so that Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 tasks are unambiguously separated (e.g., by directory name or manifest) enabling per-level evaluation as done in Table 1.
Tasks are consumable by the KernelBench prompting/evaluation pipeline as PyTorch reference source code.

Each task file's source can be read as a plain-text Python string and inserted verbatim into the one-shot prompt template (as the `<PyTorch reference architecture for specific KernelBench Problem>` slot in Appendix C.1) without additional preprocessing.

Task files import only standard PyTorch modules (e.g., `torch`, `torch.nn`, `torch.nn.functional`, `math`) so that reference execution requires no external dependencies beyond the specified PyTorch environment.
The fast_p metric, correctness checking with 5 random inputs, and wall-clock performance measurement (warmup + 100 profile iterations) are correctly implemented.
Correctness checking compares Model against ModelNew outputs on multiple randomly generated inputs of the prescribed shape and precision.

Code has been implemented that randomly generates input tensors for correctness checking by invoking the task's get_inputs() (and get_init_inputs() where relevant) with the prescribed shapes and dtypes.
Code has been implemented that sets num_correctness = 5 so that correctness is checked over exactly 5 randomly generated input sets per problem.

Code has been implemented that runs both the reference Model and the generated ModelNew on each of the 5 random inputs and compares the outputs for both shape equivalence and numerical value equivalence (within a tolerance suitable for floating point).

The correctness checker categorizes and reports failure modes distinguishing execution failures (compile-time errors, CUDA memory violations, runtime errors) from correctness errors (output shape mismatch, output value mismatch).

A kernel is marked correct only if it passes all 5 input trials (i.e., 5/5); partial-pass counts (e.g., 0/5) are treated as incorrect, matching the paper's observation that no partial correctness was observed.
Wall-clock performance is measured for nn.Module.forward on both Model and ModelNew with warmup and repeated profiling iterations.
Code has been implemented that times the forward() method of the nn.Module using torch.cuda.Event pairs to measure elapsed CUDA execution time.
Code has been implemented that performs exactly 3 warmup iterations before profiling begins, so that JIT/compilation and caching effects do not contaminate measurements.
Code has been implemented that sets num_profile = 100 profile iterations per kernel/module, recording the elapsed time of each iteration.
The profiler reports mean, min, max, and standard deviation of the 100 iteration times for both Model and ModelNew.
The evaluation ensures that only one kernel is being timed at a time on the GPU (no concurrent CUDA processes on the target device) so timing measurements are isolated.
Measured coefficient of variation (std/mean) of the 100 profiling iterations is consistently below 3% across evaluated problems, as reported in Appendix B.1.
Per-problem speedup and the fast_p metric are computed from the correctness and timing results.
Code has been implemented that computes per-problem speedup as speedup = mean(T_Model) / mean(T_ModelNew), using the mean over the 100 profile iterations for both baseline and generated kernel.

Code has been implemented for the fast_p metric defined as the fraction of tasks whose generated kernel is both functionally correct AND achieves speedup > p over the PyTorch baseline, parameterized by a user-adjustable threshold p.
fast_0 as computed by the implementation equals the pure correctness rate (fraction of tasks with a functionally correct kernel, regardless of speed).
Kernels that fail correctness (execution failure or output mismatch) are counted as speedup = 0 / not-fast for all p, and never contribute positively to fast_p regardless of measured runtime.
Code has been implemented that supports sweeping the threshold p (including p<1 and p>1) to produce the fast_p distribution curves shown in Figure 3.

Code has been implemented for the fast_p@k variant used with repeated sampling and iterative refinement, which counts a task as successful if at least one of the k samples/turns is functionally correct AND achieves speedup > p over PyTorch Eager.
The PyTorch Eager and torch.compile baselines (across multiple backends and modes) are set up and measured correctly for all 250 tasks.
PyTorch Eager baseline is implemented as the reference execution mode for all 250 KernelBench tasks.
Code has been implemented to instantiate and execute each task's reference PyTorch `Model` class in standard eager mode (no compilation, no tracing) by invoking `Model.forward(*get_inputs())`.
Code has been implemented to move both the `Model` module and its input tensors to the target CUDA device before timing so the eager baseline measures on-GPU execution.
The torch.compile baseline supports all configurations listed in Table 3 (inductor backend with default, reduce-overhead, max-autotune, max-autotune-no-cudagraphs modes, and the cudagraphs backend).
Code has been implemented to wrap each task's reference `Model` with `torch.compile(model, backend='inductor', mode='default')` to produce the default torch.compile baseline used in Table 1.
Code has been implemented to configure torch.compile with the inductor backend under mode='reduce-overhead' as one selectable baseline configuration.
Code has been implemented to configure torch.compile with the inductor backend under mode='max-autotune' as one selectable baseline configuration.
Code has been implemented to configure torch.compile with the inductor backend under mode='max-autotune-no-cudagraphs' as one selectable baseline configuration.
Code has been implemented to configure torch.compile with backend='cudagraphs' (using AOT Autograd) as one selectable baseline configuration.

Code has been implemented so the baseline runner exposes a configuration selector (e.g., a `--backend`/`--mode` argument or config dict) that maps to all six baseline configurations listed in Table 3 (Eager plus five torch.compile configurations).
torch.compile baseline timing correctly excludes compile time and captures only steady-state runtime.
Code has been implemented to perform at least one untimed warm-up forward pass on each compiled model so the initial trace/compile/autotune cost is not included in the reported runtime.

Code has been implemented so the timing loop for torch.compile baselines uses the same measurement primitives (torch.cuda.Event start/stop with `torch.cuda.synchronize`) as the eager path, and the compile step is invoked strictly before timing begins.
Baseline wall-clock measurement protocol matches the paper's specification for both Eager and torch.compile.

Code has been implemented to run 3 warm-up iterations followed by 100 timed profiling iterations of `Model.forward` for every baseline configuration, matching the num_profile=100 protocol in Appendix B.1.
Code has been implemented to record mean, min, max, and standard deviation across the 100 timed iterations and to log the coefficient of variation (std/mean) per task per baseline configuration.
The measured coefficient of variation (std/mean) for baseline wall-clock times is under 3% across tasks, matching the stability claim in Appendix B.1.
Code has been implemented to ensure baseline timing runs on an otherwise-idle GPU with a single CUDA process attached (no concurrent kernel evaluation) as specified in Appendix B.1.
Baselines are executed across all 250 tasks (Levels 1, 2, and 3) and produce a per-task baseline runtime table used downstream to compute fast_p.

Code has been implemented to iterate the baseline measurement over all 100 Level-1 tasks, all 100 Level-2 tasks, and all 50 Level-3 tasks and to store per-task baseline mean runtimes keyed by (level, task_id, baseline_config).

Code has been implemented so downstream fast_p computation loads the stored baseline runtime for the selected baseline configuration and divides it by the generated kernel runtime to obtain the per-task speedup.
Reproducing the empirical behaviour of the PyTorch baselines reported in Section B.4 and Tables 3-4.

On Level 2 and Level 3 tasks, the measured `torch.compile` (inductor, default mode) mean runtime is generally lower than the PyTorch Eager mean runtime across the majority of tasks, reproducing the observation in Appendix B.4.

On a non-trivial fraction of Level 1 tasks, the measured `torch.compile` (inductor, default mode) mean runtime exceeds the PyTorch Eager mean runtime, reproducing the small-kernel overhead effect described in Appendix B.4.

Using the DeepSeek-R1 one-shot generations, fast_1 measured against the `torch.compile` inductor default baseline reproduces the Table 1 values of 38%, 37%, and 2% for Levels 1, 2, and 3 respectively.
Using OpenAI o1 one-shot generations, fast_1 measured against the `torch.compile` inductor default baseline reproduces the Table 1 values of 28%, 19%, and 4% for Levels 1, 2, and 3 respectively.
Using DeepSeek-R1 one-shot generations, fast_1 measured against the `torch.compile` cudagraphs backend reproduces the Table 4 values of 42%, 52%, and 0% for Levels 1, 2, and 3 respectively.
Using DeepSeek-R1 one-shot generations, fast_1 measured against the `torch.compile` inductor max-autotune mode reproduces the Table 4 values of 42%, 29%, and 0% for Levels 1, 2, and 3 respectively.

depends_on: Evaluation Metric fast_p and Correctness Checking

sub_tasks.requirements: The one-shot prompting strategy with the add-operator in-context example and greedy decoding is implemented for all evaluated LMs (GPT-4o, OpenAI o1, DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1-70B/405B Instruct).
The one-shot prompt template is constructed with the required instruction text and add-operator in-context example.

Code has been implemented that assembles a one-shot prompt string containing the instruction preamble telling the model it writes custom CUDA kernels to replace PyTorch operators in the given architecture to get speedups (matching the wording in Appendix C.1).

Code has been implemented that embeds the one-shot in-context example consisting of a PyTorch reference Model with a forward that returns a+b along with get_inputs/get_init_inputs functions exactly as specified in Appendix C.1.
Code has been implemented that embeds the corresponding ModelNew example with an inline CUDA elementwise_add_kernel compiled via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline (matching Appendix C.1).

Code has been implemented that appends the target KernelBench task's PyTorch reference architecture to the prompt and includes the closing instruction requiring the model to name the output architecture ModelNew, output only code in codeblocks, no pseudocode, and no testing code.
The assembled one-shot prompt is a single query containing exactly one in-context (PyTorch reference, ModelNew) example (the add example), rather than zero-shot or multi-example prompting.
LM client bindings are implemented for every evaluated model with the correct API surface.
Code has been implemented that queries GPT-4o via the OpenAI API for the one-shot baseline.
Code has been implemented that queries OpenAI o1 via its API for the one-shot baseline.
Code has been implemented that queries DeepSeek V3 via its API for the one-shot baseline.
Code has been implemented that queries DeepSeek R1 via its API for the one-shot baseline (noting that its endpoint does not accept a temperature parameter).
Code has been implemented that queries Claude 3.5 Sonnet via the Anthropic API for the one-shot baseline.
Code has been implemented that queries Llama 3.1-70B Instruct for the one-shot baseline via a hosted inference API.
Code has been implemented that queries Llama 3.1-405B Instruct for the one-shot baseline via a hosted inference API.
Greedy decoding is used for all one-shot baseline queries where supported.
Code has been implemented that sets temperature=0 for GPT-4o, DeepSeek V3, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1-70B Instruct, and Llama 3.1-405B Instruct when producing the one-shot baseline generation.

Code has been implemented that handles reasoning models (OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1) whose API does not accept a temperature parameter by omitting it (rather than erroring), so a single deterministic sample is drawn per problem.
Exactly one sample (n=1) per KernelBench task is drawn for each model in the one-shot baseline.
The generation pipeline extracts a ModelNew implementation from the raw LM response and prepares it for evaluation.
Code has been implemented that parses the LM response and extracts the Python code from markdown codeblocks, yielding a runnable module containing a ModelNew class.
Code has been implemented that persists each model's generation for every KernelBench task/level so that generations can be evaluated and reported separately per model.
The pipeline runs the one-shot baseline over all 250 KernelBench tasks (100 Level 1, 100 Level 2, 50 Level 3) for each of the seven evaluated models.

The one-shot fast_1 results for all evaluated models across the three levels (over both PyTorch Eager and torch.compile baselines), the failure-mode breakdown, and the speedup distributions match the paper.

The one-shot evaluation pipeline runs all seven models (GPT-4o, OpenAI o1, DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1-70B Instruct, Llama 3.1-405B Instruct) over all 250 KernelBench tasks (Level 1, 2, 3) on NVIDIA L40S and produces fast_1 tables comparing to PyTorch Eager and torch.compile baselines.

Code has been implemented that iterates the one-shot generation+evaluation pipeline over every KernelBench task in Levels 1, 2, and 3 and stores per-task generated code, correctness result, PyTorch Eager runtime, torch.compile runtime, and generated-kernel runtime.

Code has been implemented that dispatches one-shot generation for each of the seven evaluated models (GPT-4o, OpenAI o1, DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1-70B Instruct, Llama 3.1-405B Instruct) using the correct API endpoint / model identifier and greedy decoding (temperature=0).

Code has been implemented that aggregates per-task speedups into a fast_1 score (percentage of tasks where the LM-generated kernel is correct and strictly faster than the reference baseline runtime) and computes it separately against PyTorch Eager and against torch.compile (default inductor configuration).

Code has been implemented that emits Table 1 as a structured artifact (e.g., CSV/JSON/Markdown) with rows for the seven models and columns fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager on Levels 1/2/3 and fast_1 vs torch.compile on Levels 1/2/3.
Reported fast_1 values against PyTorch Eager match the paper's Table 1.
GPT-4o achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 4% on Level 1, 5% on Level 2, and 0% on Level 3.
OpenAI o1 achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 10% on Level 1, 24% on Level 2, and 12% on Level 3.
DeepSeek V3 achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 6% on Level 1, 4% on Level 2, and 8% on Level 3.
DeepSeek R1 achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 12% on Level 1, 36% on Level 2, and 2% on Level 3.
Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 10% on Level 1, 7% on Level 2, and 2% on Level 3.
Llama 3.1-70B Instruct achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 3% on Level 1, 0% on Level 2, and 0% on Level 3.
Llama 3.1-405B Instruct achieves the reported fast_1 vs PyTorch Eager of 3% on Level 1, 0% on Level 2, and 2% on Level 3.
Reported fast_1 values against torch.compile (default inductor) match Table 1.
GPT-4o achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 18% on Level 1, 4% on Level 2, and 4% on Level 3.
OpenAI o1 achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 28% on Level 1, 19% on Level 2, and 4% on Level 3.
DeepSeek V3 achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 20% on Level 1, 2% on Level 2, and 2% on Level 3.
DeepSeek R1 achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 38% on Level 1, 37% on Level 2, and 2% on Level 3.
Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 29% on Level 1, 2% on Level 2, and 2% on Level 3.
Llama 3.1-70B Instruct achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 11% on Level 1, 0% on Level 2, and 0% on Level 3.
Llama 3.1-405B Instruct achieves the reported fast_1 vs torch.compile (default) of 16% on Level 1, 0% on Level 2, and 0% on Level 3.

The failure-mode categorization pipeline (Figure 2) classifies every non-correct one-shot generation into execution failure vs. functional correctness failure and reproduces the paper's reported per-model breakdown.

Code has been implemented that classifies each generation as one of {correct, execution_failure, functional_correctness_failure}, where execution_failure covers CUDA/nvcc/Python compile-time errors, CUDA memory access violations, and runtime errors, and functional_correctness_failure covers output-tensor shape mismatches and output-value mismatches.

Code has been implemented that aggregates the failure-mode classifications per model per level and emits a stacked bar chart reproducing Figure 2 (execution failure vs. functional correctness vs. correct percentages).
The reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 each produce fewer than 55% incorrect generations in the one-shot setting (aggregated across levels), matching the paper's claim.

Each of the non-reasoning models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek V3, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1-70B, Llama 3.1-405B) produces more than 70% incorrect generations in the one-shot setting (aggregated across levels), matching the paper's claim.

The functional-correctness failure rate (fraction of generations that execute successfully but produce wrong outputs) is comparable across all evaluated LMs — no model differs from the mean functional-correctness failure rate by an amount substantially larger than the paper's stated 'all LMs struggle with functional correctness to a similar degree'.
The fast_p speedup-distribution curves (Figure 3) are computed and match the paper's qualitative and quantitative claims.

Code has been implemented that sweeps p over a range including at least {0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2} (and extends to larger p) and computes fast_p for each (model, level) pair using PyTorch Eager as the baseline.
Code has been implemented that plots fast_p vs threshold p as three subplots (one per KernelBench level), overlaying curves for each evaluated model, reproducing the layout of Figure 3.
The fast_p curves are monotonically non-increasing in p for every (model, level) pair.
At p=1, fewer than 15% of LM-generated kernels outperform the PyTorch Eager baseline across every KernelBench level (aggregated over all seven models), matching Section 4.3.

The reasoning-based LMs (OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1) achieve strictly higher fast_1 than the non-reasoning LMs on Levels 1 and 2 when aggregated over the one-shot baseline, matching Section 4.3's claim that reasoning LMs generally outperform other LMs in providing speedups.
The per-model speedup distributions of correct kernels (Figure 7 box-and-whisker) are produced and reproduce the paper's per-level distribution characteristics.

Code has been implemented that, for each (model, level) pair, collects the speedup = T_Model / T_ModelNew ratios for all functionally correct one-shot generations and stores them as a distribution suitable for box-and-whisker plotting.

Code has been implemented that renders a box-and-whisker plot (matching Figure 7's layout, one subplot per level) showing correct-kernel speedup distributions per model, annotated with the correctness rate (percentage of correctly generated kernels) next to each model name.
The median speedup over PyTorch Eager for correct one-shot kernels is below 1.0 for Level 1 and below 1.0 for Level 3 (aggregated across models), matching Section B.3.
The median speedup over PyTorch Eager for correct one-shot kernels on Level 2 is slightly above 1.0 (aggregated across models), matching Section B.3.
The Level 1 speedup distribution contains at least one outlier correct kernel whose speedup over PyTorch Eager exceeds 10x, matching Section B.3's observation.
The paper's headline aggregate claims about one-shot results across all levels are verified from the reproduced numbers.

OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 each match the PyTorch Eager baseline (i.e., fast_1) on fewer than 20% of KernelBench tasks when averaged/aggregated across the three levels, matching the abstract and Section 1 claim.
Averaged across the seven evaluated LMs and the three levels, the fast_1 rate over PyTorch Eager in the one-shot setting is below 20%, matching Section 4.1's summary.
DeepSeek R1 achieves the highest fast_1 on Level 2 (36% over PyTorch Eager) among all evaluated models in the one-shot baseline, matching Table 1.
OpenAI o1 achieves the highest fast_1 on Level 3 (12% over PyTorch Eager) among all evaluated models in the one-shot baseline, matching Table 1.

depends_on: One-Shot Baseline Prompt and LM Generation Pipeline
Evaluation Metric fast_p and Correctness Checking

sub_tasks.requirements: Kernel generations from Section 4 evaluated across GPU platforms (L40S, A10G, and others) reproduce the paper's finding that one-shot LM-generated kernels do not generalize well across hardware.
Cross-hardware evaluation infrastructure is set up to run the one-shot generated kernels from Section 4 on multiple GPU platforms.

Code has been implemented to load the exact set of one-shot LM-generated kernels (from Section 4.1, greedy-decoded across the evaluated LMs) as the artifacts to be re-evaluated on alternative GPU platforms without regeneration.

Code has been implemented to target evaluation on at least NVIDIA L40S and NVIDIA A10G GPUs (the two platforms explicitly compared in Section 4.4/Figure 9), with a configurable device selection so additional GPUs referenced in Table 14/Figure 8 can be added.

Code has been implemented so that on every target GPU the same correctness protocol (5 random inputs) and timing protocol (3 warmup + 100 profiled trials, mean wall-clock time) is used, ensuring speedups are computed consistently across hardware.
The per-GPU PyTorch Eager baseline runtime is (re)measured on each target GPU rather than reused across GPUs, so the fast_1 metric on that GPU is computed against its own baseline.
The cross-hardware fast_p aggregation and reporting pipeline produces the tables and figures analogous to Table 14, Figure 8, and Figure 9.
Code has been implemented to compute fast_1 per (model, KernelBench level, GPU) triple, producing the cross-hardware table analogous to Table 14 covering Levels 1, 2, and 3.

Code has been implemented to plot the Level 1 cross-hardware speedup comparison (analogous to Figure 8) showing that kernels which outperform PyTorch Eager on L40S achieve similar speedups on the other evaluated GPUs.
Code has been implemented to plot the Level 2 cross-hardware speedup comparison (analogous to Figure 9) that visualizes the larger per-problem speedup variation across GPUs for Level 2 kernels.

Code has been implemented to emit a per-problem, per-GPU speedup record (kernel id, model, level, GPU, correctness flag, baseline time, kernel time, speedup) so that Figures 8-9 and Table 14 can be regenerated and audited from a single source of truth.
The reproduced numbers demonstrate the paper's specific cross-hardware (non-)generalization claims.
DeepSeek-R1 one-shot fast_1 on KernelBench Level 2 measured on NVIDIA L40S matches the paper's reported value of 36%.
DeepSeek-R1 one-shot fast_1 on KernelBench Level 2 measured on NVIDIA A10G matches the paper's reported value of 47%, reproducing the L40S-vs-A10G gap that motivates the non-generalization claim.

For KernelBench Level 1, the reproduced results show that the set of one-shot kernels outperforming PyTorch Eager on L40S achieves similar (correlated) speedups on the other evaluated GPUs, consistent with Table 14 / Figure 8.

For KernelBench Level 2, the reproduced per-problem speedups exhibit noticeably larger variation across GPUs than for Level 1 (quantified e.g. via per-problem speedup standard deviation or rank correlation across GPUs), consistent with Figure 9 and the paper's conclusion that one-shot LM-generated kernels do not generalize well across hardware.
The reproduced cross-hardware fast_1 table (analogous to Table 14) matches the paper's reported entries for all (model, level, GPU) combinations reported in that table within tolerance.

The repeated sampling method (fast_p@k with k up to 100) using high-temperature sampling for DeepSeek-V3 (temp 1.6) and Llama 3.1-70B (temp 0.7) is implemented and reproduces the paper's improvement trends.
The repeated sampling pipeline is implemented to draw k parallel samples per KernelBench task and compute fast_p@k.
Code has been implemented that queries the LM with the same one-shot baseline prompt (add-operator in-context example) used in Section 4.1 for repeated sampling, per Appendix C.2.
Code has been implemented that draws k independent samples per KernelBench task from the target LM API, supporting k up to 100.
The sampling temperature is set to 1.6 for DeepSeek-V3 and 0.7 for Llama 3.1-70B Instruct, matching Appendix C.2.
Code has been implemented that evaluates every one of the k samples for correctness (5 random inputs) and wall-clock speedup against PyTorch Eager on the target GPU.
Code has been implemented that computes fast_p@k, defined as the fraction of tasks for which at least one of the k samples is correct and achieves speedup > p over PyTorch Eager.
The fast_p@k computation supports evaluation at intermediate values of k (e.g., 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100) so the fast_1@k curve versus k can be plotted as in Figure 4.
The repeated sampling experiments are run across all three KernelBench levels for both DeepSeek-V3 and Llama 3.1-70B Instruct.

The GPU orchestrator for parallel generation/evaluation (CPU pre-compilation of kernels, GPU semaphore acquisition, safe handling of illegal memory accesses / deadlocks / timeouts) and the kernel-inspection UI are implemented.
The evaluation orchestrator implements a multi-process finite state machine that overlaps kernel generation with kernel execution, keeping GPU access strictly gated by a semaphore process.

Code has been implemented that launches multiple worker processes (one per KernelBench task or trajectory) which independently drive the multi-turn iterative refinement / repeated sampling state machine.

Code has been implemented for a dedicated GPU-broker process that owns semaphore(s) representing the available physical GPUs and hands them out to worker processes only for the kernel-execution/profiling state.

Worker processes acquire a GPU via the semaphore only during kernel execution/profiling and release it immediately afterwards so that GPU wall-time occupancy is not held during LM generation or CPU-only phases.
Kernel compilation is offloaded to CPU workers ahead of GPU execution to avoid processes hogging GPU time during nvcc invocation.
Code has been implemented that invokes nvcc on the CPU to pre-compile each LM-generated CUDA source into a binary/loadable extension for the target hardware before any GPU semaphore is acquired.
The pre-compilation step captures and returns nvcc compilation errors as a distinct failure mode without ever acquiring a GPU, so that compile-failing generations do not consume GPU time.
The orchestrator safely handles unavoidable kernel-execution faults (CUDA illegal memory accesses, deadlocks, hangs) without crashing the overall run.
Kernel execution is run in an isolated child process so that a CUDA illegal memory access or fatal driver error terminates only that subprocess while the parent orchestrator continues.

A per-kernel wall-clock timeout is enforced and, on expiry, the runner terminates the offending process, releases its GPU semaphore, and records the failure with the message 'Your kernel execution timed out'.
When a worker process dies or hangs, the orchestrator releases its held GPU semaphore and spawns a replacement worker so overall throughput is preserved.

Distinct failure categories (compile error, runtime error, illegal memory access, timeout/deadlock, correctness mismatch) are captured as structured status codes in the evaluation output rather than being conflated.
A kernel-inspection UI (as depicted in Figure 12) is provided for visualizing and comparing kernel generation trajectories.
Code has been implemented for a visual interface that displays the generated kernel source code for each task alongside its measured performance (runtime, speedup, correctness status).
The UI supports comparing kernel generations across different techniques/configurations (e.g., one-shot vs. iterative refinement, different models) side-by-side for the same KernelBench task.

The UI exposes per-turn trajectory inspection for iterative refinement runs, showing the sequence of generations G together with the associated execution feedback E and profiler feedback P at each turn.

depends_on: Evaluation Metric fast_p and Correctness Checking
